967.title: Volozhin
967.hook: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin founds a new kind of yeshiva
967.howItsDone: In yeshivas today, students commonly study Talmud in pairs called chavruta, reading aloud and debating each line, in a shared hall called the beit midrash.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Vilna Gaon, who lived inside his books and opposed the new Hasidic movement. Your line was the genius of vilna. Today, one of his students opens a door.

A long wooden table. Two young men bent over one open book, both talking at once. One reads a line aloud in a singsong. The other shakes his head: no, that can't be what it means, look at the next word. They argue, they laugh, they go back to the line. Down the table, pair after pair is doing the same. It sounds more like a market than a library. Someone passing the door might think a fight had broken out. It hasn't. This is serious study, in a hall in a small town called Volozhin.
screen: `TWO YOUNG MEN, ONE BOOK.` → `BOTH TALKING AT ONCE.` → `A HALL THAT SOUNDS LIKE A MARKET.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin had been a student of the Vilna Gaon. He took his teacher's love of study and gave it a building. Histories remember it as a new kind of academy: one that gathered students from many places, who left home to live and learn there, supported by gifts from Jewish communities far beyond Volozhin itself. In a sense, it belonged to everyone who paid for it. Tradition says the sound of learning in its hall was meant never to stop, day or night, with students taking turns. Why did that matter? In his book Nefesh HaChaim, Chaim teaches that Torah study is not only good for the person studying; it helps hold the whole world in being. Seen that way, a hall where learning never stops is a kind of watch kept for the world. And notice how the learning happens: in pairs, out loud, arguing. Proverbs has a line for it, in the King James wording: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." The Talmud, in tractate Taanit, reads that verse about two students of Torah, who sharpen each other like two blades. In the same passage a rabbi says he learned much from his teachers, more from his friends, and most of all from his students. That is the idea of the yeshiva: you learn Torah across a table, from someone who refuses to let your first answer stand.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who has sharpened you: a friend who argued back, a coworker who asked the question you missed, a child who asked why. Picture the two of you at a table with something open between you, and ask what they showed you that you couldn't see alone.
Yeshiva. An academy for the study of Torah and Talmud, where students often learn in pairs, out loud. Volozhin's gathered students from many places. Today's word.

968.title: The Pale
968.hook: the Russian Empire confines most Jews to its western provinces
968.howItsDone: Jews who keep Shabbat by traditional law observe the techum, staying within a set walking distance of the town where they spend the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Volozhin: two students over one book, sharpening each other like iron. Your line was the yeshiva. Today, the map that yeshiva sat on.

A Jewish trader has goods to sell in a city a few days' ride to the east. The roads are open, the horse is ready, the buyers are waiting. And he cannot simply go. No wall stands in his way, no river. The line he cannot cross is written in a law, drawn on a map in an office far away. On one side, he may live, trade, marry and be buried. On the other, for him, the road ends, unless an official grants a permit he may never get. His Christian neighbor can take that road tomorrow. Today, a boundary with a name: the Pale.
screen: `A ROAD THAT IS OPEN.` → `A LINE WRITTEN IN A LAW.` → `ON THE OTHER SIDE, THE ROAD ENDS.`

segments.voice: When the Russian Empire took over lands that had belonged to Poland, it took over their Jewish communities too, the world of the Council of Four Lands, the Baal Shem Tov and the Vilna Gaon. The empire's answer was a boundary. Jews were, with some exceptions, allowed to live only in its western provinces, and kept out of the Russian heartland and its great cities. That region came to be called the Pale of Settlement. Inside it, life was crowded and often poor, but also full: market towns, study houses, Hasidic courts, the yeshiva at Volozhin. A whole Yiddish-speaking world grew up inside a line someone else had drawn. In Hebrew and Yiddish the Pale had its own name, techum ha-moshav, the boundary of settlement. And techum, boundary, already meant something in Jewish life: the limit on how far a person walks on Shabbat. It goes back to a verse about the manna in the wilderness. In the JPS translation of Exodus, the Israelites are told: "abide ye every man in his place, let no man go out of his place on the seventh day." The rabbis read that as a measured distance around a town. So Jews in the Pale knew two boundaries by the same name. One was chosen, taken on as holy rest, and lifted every week when Shabbat ended. The other was imposed by a government that did not want them, and did not lift at sunset. One limit was a gift you kept. The other was a fence kept around you.
screen: `THE EMPIRE DRAWS A LINE.` · `A WHOLE WORLD INSIDE IT.` · `TECHUM — THE SHABBAT BOUNDARY.` · then, large: `ONE CHOSEN, ONE IMPOSED.`

segments.voice: Think of where your feet can take you without asking anyone's permission, a store, a friend's street, another town, and let one place come clearly to mind. Then, gently, remember the trader at the edge of the Pale, horse ready and nowhere to ride, and hold both pictures.

Your line: a fence kept around you. Not every boundary is a gift. See you tomorrow.

969.title: The cantonists
969.hook: Jewish boys are conscripted into the Russian army for a lifetime of service
969.howItsDone: The cantonists are remembered in Yiddish songs, memoirs and later histories, and some Jewish families still tell stories of ancestors who were taken or who hid their sons.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Pale, a line in law a trader could not ride past. Today, the hardest thing the empire took from inside that line.

Some songs are sung so a child will fall asleep. Others are sung so a child will be remembered. In the Yiddish-speaking towns of the Russian Empire, there were songs of the second kind: a boy snatched from his bed at night, a mother running after a wagon, men who came for the children of the poor. They are memories set to a tune, about a real law and real boys. A gentle warning: today is about children taken from their families.
screen: `SONGS SO A CHILD WILL BE REMEMBERED.` → `A BOY SNATCHED AT NIGHT.` → `A REAL LAW, REAL BOYS.`

segments.voice: Under Tsar Nicholas the First, the Russian Empire began drafting Jews into its army, and it did something especially cruel with Jewish boys. Boys not yet old enough to be soldiers could be taken anyway and sent to military schools for soldiers' children, called cantonist schools, often far from home. The service that followed was so long that a boy taken as a child might come home a grown man, if he came home at all. In those schools, boys were pressed, sometimes brutally, to be baptized and leave Judaism behind. Some held on. Some could not. And part of this story is painful to tell, and Jewish memory tells it honestly. The empire made each Jewish community hand over its own quota of recruits, so the choosing fell on the community's leaders. Too often, the sons of the poor and the orphans were handed over, and men called khappers, snatchers, were hired to seize boys when families hid them. The wound ran outward, against the empire, and inward too. The prophet Jeremiah gave this grief its words: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Rachel, the matriarch, weeping for children who are gone. And the next verse answers her: "they shall come again from the land of the enemy." Some cantonists did come back, some having kept their faith in secret all those years. Their stories, and the songs, are how a people refused to let those boys be forgotten.

970.title: Mussar begins
970.hook: Rabbi Israel Salanter starts a movement of ethical self-work
970.howItsDone: People who practice mussar today often study a classic ethical text in a small group or with a partner, choose one middah to focus on for a stretch of weeks, and keep a short journal of how it went.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cantonists, and Rachel weeping for her children. Your line was the taken children. Today, a quieter story from the same world: a rabbi who turned study inward.

The story starts with a boot. A shoemaker is mending it late at night, by a candle that has almost burned down, when a rabbi passing in the street stops at his door and asks why he's still at it. The shoemaker shrugs: as long as the candle is burning, there's still time to mend. Tradition says the rabbi walked away repeating it to himself, like a verse. The rabbi was Israel Salanter, and that is the heart of what he started.
screen: `A BOOT, LATE AT NIGHT.` → `A SHOEMAKER AND A CANDLE.` → `THERE'S STILL TIME TO MEND.`

segments.voice: Rabbi Israel Salanter came out of the Lithuanian world of learning we've been visiting, the world of the Vilna Gaon and the yeshiva. He looked at people who knew the law brilliantly and asked an awkward question. Knowing what is right is one thing. Becoming someone who does it, when you're tired, irritated, tempted, is another. So he urged people to study mussar. The word appears in Proverbs, where the King James Bible renders it as instruction: "My son, hear the instruction of thy father." For Salanter, mussar meant teaching aimed at your own character. He encouraged people to set aside time, alone or together in a room set apart for it, to read ethical works slowly and with feeling, often saying a single line aloud over and over until it sank from the mind into the heart. Not to collect knowledge. To change. The Hebrew name for a trait of character is middah, a measure: patience, honesty, humility, anger, generosity. Mussar works on one middah at a time, the way a craftsman fixes one seam, then the next. And it is honest about how slow that is. In the Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, Hillel warns people not to trust in themselves until the day they die. That sounds grim, but in mussar it is closer to hopeful: the work is never finished, so it's never too late to start. Salanter's students carried this into the yeshivas, and some of those yeshivas made mussar study part of every day.
screen: `KNOWING IS NOT BECOMING.` · `MUSSAR — INSTRUCTION FOR THE SELF.` · `ONE MIDDAH AT A TIME.` · then, large: `WHILE THE CANDLE BURNS, YOU CAN MEND.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself, without judging, which one middah, one habit of the heart, has been costing you lately: impatience, sharpness with someone you love, putting things off. Give it a short phrase in your own words, like "slow down before I answer," and repeat it quietly, the way Salanter's students repeated a line, until it feels less like an idea and more like a habit.

971.title: Moses Mendelssohn
971.hook: a Berlin philosopher who translated the Torah into German
971.howItsDone: Mendelssohn's German translation of the Torah, with its Hebrew commentary known as the Biur, is studied by historians as a turning point, and his life is often discussed in Jewish schools as a model and a question about living in two cultures.

segments.voice: Yesterday, mussar: a shoemaker's candle, and Salanter's idea that there's still time to mend. Your line was work on yourself. Today we leave Eastern Europe for Berlin.

The challenge is printed on the first pages of a book, where anyone can read it. A Swiss pastor named Johann Caspar Lavater has dedicated the book to a Jewish philosopher in Berlin, and challenges him in public: either show what is wrong with Christianity, or do what reason demands and be baptized. Readers are watching. The philosopher is admired in the salons, praised by Christian friends, read in German. Now he must choose between attacking his neighbors' faith and leaving his own. His name is Moses Mendelssohn.
screen: `A PUBLIC CHALLENGE.` → `REFUTE IT, OR BE BAPTIZED.` → `READERS WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Mendelssohn took a third way. He wrote back, publicly, that he remained firm in his own faith and had no wish to go to war against anyone else's. Judaism, he explained, does not go out looking for converts, and he did not want to spend his life in religious dispute. He would keep his faith and keep his friends. That answer is Mendelssohn in miniature: a man living in two worlds and refusing to give either up. He was an observant Jew who kept the commandments, and a German philosopher who wrote in elegant German about God, the soul and beauty. Then he brought those two worlds into one room. He translated the Torah into German and had it printed in Hebrew letters, alongside the Hebrew text and a Hebrew commentary. A young Jew who read Hebrew could open the Torah and, line by line, learn a careful German too. There's an old rabbinic way of thinking about that kind of bridge. In Genesis, Noah blesses Shem and Japheth: "God shall enlarge Japheth, and he shall dwell in the tents of Shem." The Talmud, in tractate Megillah, reads that verse as permission to write the Torah in Greek, letting the beauty of Japheth live inside the tents of Shem. Mendelssohn's translation made a similar wager: that a new language could live inside the Torah's tent without knocking it down. Not everyone agreed. Some rabbis worried it would lead young people toward German and away from Torah. Others welcomed it. Both reactions are part of his story.

972.title: The Haskalah
972.hook: the Jewish Enlightenment, joining Jewish and general learning
972.howItsDone: The Haskalah's legacy lives on in modern Hebrew literature and in Jewish schools that teach both Jewish and general subjects, while some traditional communities still keep secular learning at a distance.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses Mendelssohn: the Torah in German, printed in Hebrew letters, and a man living in two worlds. Your line was two worlds. Today, the movement that grew up around people like him.

How do you say telescope in the language of the Psalms? Or vaccine, or electricity, or newspaper? The Bible never needed those words. Hebrew had long been a language of prayer, study and law, while people spoke something else at home. Then a group of Jewish writers decided Hebrew should be able to talk about everything: planets and poetry, chemistry and history. They printed journals in Hebrew about science, and wrote Hebrew poems that had nothing to do with the synagogue. They were stretching an ancient language to fit a new world.
screen: `TELESCOPE, IN THE LANGUAGE OF THE PSALMS?` → `HEBREW FOR EVERYTHING.` → `AN ANCIENT LANGUAGE, A NEW WORLD.`

segments.voice: The movement is called the Haskalah, the Jewish Enlightenment, and its followers were maskilim. It began among Jews in Germany in Mendelssohn's circle, and later moved east, into the towns and cities of the Pale. The maskilim had a program. Jews, they said, should learn the languages of the countries they lived in, and mathematics, science, history and useful trades, alongside the Torah, not instead of it. They wanted Jewish schools that taught both, and Hebrew itself reborn as a living language of literature. They liked to point back to scholars like Maimonides, who studied philosophy and medicine and wrote some of the great works of Jewish law. An old line in the Mishnah fits their hopes. In Pirkei Avot, Ben Zoma asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. Wisdom, on that reading, can come from anywhere, and a learned Jew can take it in without losing who they are. That was the maskilim's bet. Not everyone accepted it, and the argument was fierce. Traditional rabbis, Hasidic and non-Hasidic alike, warned that the Haskalah was a road out of Judaism, and could point to young people who walked it all the way out. Some maskilim, in turn, mocked the traditional world, sometimes cruelly. Each camp had its own picture of Jewish life in a new age. Meanwhile the Hebrew journals kept printing, stretching the language of the Psalms to name things it had never named before.
screen: `THE MASKILIM AND THEIR PROGRAM.` · `TORAH AND THE WORLD'S LEARNING.` · `WHO IS WISE? WHO LEARNS FROM EVERYONE.` · then, large: `A FIERCE ARGUMENT, AND HEBREW STRETCHING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something from the ordinary world you know a little about: how plants grow, how money works, a piece of music, a law of physics. Turn it slowly, the way a maskil might, and ask what a Torah teacher would find worth noticing in it, a pattern, a kind of order, a question about how to live; you don't need an answer.
Haskalah. The Jewish Enlightenment: joining Torah with general learning, and reviving Hebrew as a language for everything. Its followers were the maskilim. Today's word.

973.title: Citizens (1791)
973.carry: a door opened, with a price

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Haskalah: Hebrew stretched to talk about telescopes, and Ben Zoma learning from everyone. Your line was enlightenment. Today the week closes with a vote.

A hall in Paris, crowded and loud. The French Revolution has torn up the old order, and the new assembly has declared that men are born free and equal in rights. Now a hard question is on the floor: does that include the Jews? Some deputies say yes, obviously. Others say Jews are a separate nation and can never be truly French. The debate goes back and forth, session after session. A people who have lived behind lines drawn by others wait to hear whether a line is about to be erased. Today, one word: citizens.
screen: `FREE AND EQUAL IN RIGHTS.` → `DOES THAT INCLUDE THE JEWS?` → `A LINE ABOUT TO BE ERASED?`

segments.voice: The answer, in the end, was yes. Revolutionary France made Jews full citizens, with the same rights as anyone else: to live where they chose, to work in any trade, to vote. For Jews in France, it changed daily life. But it came with a bargain, and one deputy, Count Stanislas de Clermont-Tonnerre, put it bluntly. Roughly: to the Jews as a nation, nothing; to the Jews as individuals, everything. You may be equal, one by one, but not as a community that governs itself. Remember the Council of Four Lands, and the Jewish courts and councils that had run Jewish life? Citizenship asked Jews to hand much of that to the state, and become French citizens of the Jewish faith. Some welcomed that as freedom at last. Others worried about what a people loses when it becomes only a religion. The Torah has its own line about equal law, though there it is a command to Israel about the stranger among them. In Leviticus, the King James Bible reads: "Ye shall have one manner of law, as well for the stranger, as for one of your own country." In Europe, Jews had long been the strangers. Now a country offered them one manner of law. That closes a week of boundaries: Volozhin, the Pale, the cantonists, Salanter, Mendelssohn and the maskilim, and now a vote that opened a door, with a price attached.
screen: `FULL CITIZENS, EQUAL IN RIGHTS.` · `AS INDIVIDUALS, EVERYTHING.` · `ONE MANNER OF LAW.` · then, large: `A DOOR OPENED, WITH A PRICE.`

segments.voice: Think of one right you have where you live that you rarely think about: to vote, to move, to speak, to worship or not to worship; if you're not a citizen there, think of one protection you do have. Let it become concrete, and remember the people in that Paris hall, waiting to hear whether that right was theirs. If you pray, you can give thanks for it in your own words.
Citizens. Revolutionary France made Jews full and equal citizens, as individuals, asking them to become French citizens of the Jewish faith. Today's word.
Your line: a door opened, with a price. Equal as individuals, not as a nation. That's the week.
